fields.Front: What are the two main parts of an object, and what is each also called?
fields.Back: Attributes (also called data members): the information the object stores. Behaviours (also called member functions or methods): the actions it can perform. Data and the operations on that data travel together.

fields.Front: Define class and object using the slides' Car example.
fields.Back: A class is a blueprint/template defining the properties and behaviours of an object; an object is an instance of a class. Car is the class; specific cars (a Ford, a Toyota) are objects. The class is the type, the object is a value of that type.

fields.Front: What are attributes, where are they declared, and what are the Car examples?
fields.Back: Variables that store information about the object, declared inside the class body in C++. For Car: color, speed, model. Each object gets its own storage, so changing one car's speed does not change another's.

fields.Front: What do methods define, and what are the Car examples?
fields.Back: The behaviour of an object, i.e. what actions it can perform. For Car: accelerate(), brake(), getSpeed(). Methods live inside the class and have direct access to that object's attributes. A method that only reads an attribute is a getter; one that changes it is a setter.

fields.Front: In the slides' Car class, what does Car(std::string carModel, int carYear) do and how do you know it is a constructor?
fields.Back: It assigns model = carModel; and year = carYear;, copying the arguments into the object's private attributes. It is a constructor because it has the class's name and no return type.

fields.Front: Why does myCar.year = 1999; fail to compile for the slides' Car class, and what would you add to allow it?
fields.Back: year is declared under private:, so no code outside the class may read or write it. To allow the change you add a public setter (e.g. setYear(int)) that can also validate the value; that is the mechanical basis for encapsulation.

fields.Front: Why is double getBalance() const marked const, and what breaks if you drop it?
fields.Back: const promises the compiler and the reader that calling it does not modify the object; getters should always be const. Without it, the getter cannot be called on a const Account or through a const reference, so callers that hold the object read-only fail to compile.

fields.Front: What classic compile error follows a C++ class definition?
fields.Back: Forgetting the semicolon after the closing brace: the definition must end };, not }.

fields.Front: Give the Week 1 preview definition of encapsulation and say which half does the real work.
fields.Back: Bundling data (attributes) and methods (behaviours) into a single unit (the object) AND restricting direct access to some of the object's components. The second half is what gives it power: since state is private, every change must go through a method that can validate it.

fields.Front: If you create Car myCar("Toyota", 2022); and Car otherCar("Ford", 2018);, what do they share and what is separate?
fields.Back: They share the same class definition and therefore the same set of methods, but each object has its own copy of the attributes (model, year). That is exactly the class/instance distinction.

fields.Text: Access specifiers: {{c1::private}} = only code inside the class; {{c1::public}} = any code inside or outside; {{c1::protected}} = the class and its derived classes, used in inheritance.
fields.Extra: Members of a C++ class are private by default.

fields.Text: In a C++ class, members written before any access specifier are {{c1::private}} by default.
fields.Extra: That is why the slides' Shape example, which has no public: label, has a private draw().

fields.Text: A {{c1::constructor}} initializes an object (same name as the class, no return type); a {{c1::destructor}} cleans up resources when the object is destroyed (named {{c1::~ClassName()}}, no arguments).
fields.Extra: Constructors put the object in a valid state; destructors free memory, close files, release resources. Both run automatically.
The arguments in parentheses go to the constructor; displayInfo() is called with the dot operator on the object.

fields.Text: Account(double initialBalance) : balance(initialBalance) {} initializes the member with a {{c1::member initializer list}}, which is preferred over assignment in the constructor body because it {{c1::initializes the member directly instead of default-constructing then assigning}}.

{{c1::Inheritance}} lets one class derive properties and behaviours from another; {{c1::Polymorphism}} lets one interface be used for different data types or classes, e.g. function {{c1::overloading}} and {{c1::overriding}}.
fields.Extra: Both are previews for the Week 2 lecture.

fields.Text: Compile-time polymorphism covers {{c1::function overloading}} and {{c1::operator overloading}}; run-time polymorphism happens through {{c1::virtual functions}}.
fields.Extra: From the speaker notes on the Polymorphism advantage slide.

fields.Text: An object's two parts: {{c1::attributes}}, also called {{c1::data members}}, and {{c1::behaviors}}, also called member functions or {{c1::methods}}.
A {{c1::class}} is the blueprint or template; an {{c1::object}} is an instance of it. For the class Car, a specific Toyota is an {{c1::object}}.
In Car myCar("Toyota", 2022); the arguments are passed to the {{c1::constructor}}, and myCar.displayInfo() reaches the method through the {{c1::dot operator}}.
fields.Extra: displayInfo() can read the private model and year because it is a member of the class.

fields.Text: A C++ class definition must end with a closing brace followed by a {{c1::semicolon}} - omitting it is a classic compile error.
